Good afternoon, colleagues. This afternoon, the Forum will hear 3 sets of panel presentations. For the first set of panel presentations, I am pleased to welcome the distinguished presenters from Germany, Kazakhstan, and Seychelles. Before I begin, I would like to appeal to the presenting countries to adhere to the agreed 10 minutes per presentation to allow sufficient time for all presenters as well as engagement with other states and participants. I apologize in advance if I have to interrupt speakers, and I hope that I will not come to that point, and with your cooperation. Given the number of countries making BNR presentations at this year's HLPIA, I believe that we all understand the need to be disciplined so as to allow adequate time for presentations as well as interactions from the floor. With this, the Forum will now hear the Voluntary National Review by Germany, Now I invite Her Excellency Bärbel Kofler, Parliamentary State Secretary to the Federal Minister for Economic Cooperation and Development of Germany, and Her Excellency Ms. Rita Swaraj Jalur Suta, Parliamentary State Secretary to the Federal Ministry for the Environment, Climate Action, for Nature Conservation and Nuclear Safety of Germany to make a presentation. Your Excellency, you have the floor now.

Thank you, President. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen. Germany is sending a clear message with this third VNR: participation works. Because sustainable development can only succeed with broad public support that is taken seriously by policymakers. Germany is truly practicing participation. Young people, along with stakeholders from civil society, business, science, the federal states, and municipalities were all involved in drafting our VNR, as well as the German Sustainable Development Strategy. New perspectives emerge from dialogue. These have become part of our Sustainable Development Strategy and the VNR, play a key role in ambitious and widely accepted goals for progress on sustainable development in Germany. We must thank our stakeholders warmly. They have made a major contribution to the quality of the overall VNR. Collective commitment is the only way to make accelerated implementation of the Sustainable Development Goals a reality. International exchange and peer learning also helps by spark innovation, transfer good practices, and prevent mistakes. This accelerated SDG implementation. Together with our partner countries Finland, Guatemala, Indonesia, Nigeria, Thailand, and South Africa, we forge a partnership of peer learning focused on accelerating progress. Exchange about processes, content, and challenges enriched our VNR. We are looking forward to continuing this exchange, especially with the countries that will present their VNR 2026. Trust and dialogue will be key for the SDGs in the coming years. We are committed to continuing down this path, peer learning in close partnerships. Participation combined with integrated critical SDG monitoring generates ambition and provides direction for SDG implementation. Following the recommendations of the Global Sustainable Development Report, Germany has identified 6 areas of transformation and 5 levers for advancing systemic change and measurably speeding up implementation of the 2030 Agenda. Circular economy is one of the German areas of transformation for integrated SDG implementation. We have a national strategy for promoting efficient resource use, minimising waste, and protecting our environment. We use digital solutions to support informed consumer choices, In addition, we are extending product lifecycles by providing digital information on materials, origin, and disposal. We are also investing in research and developing new technologies to prevent greenhouse gas emissions. Our vision is a circular economy that benefits the environment and people. Thank you.

Well, it's a shared effort, so I'm continuing. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, Germany's feminist development policy, which is part of the German Sustainable Development Strategy, is one of the instruments that brings to life our engagement for the SDGs. In order to advance gender equality, Germany is working together with its partner countries. We are pursuing an international policy that is aligned with this 3 Rs: equal rights, equal access to resources, and equal representation for women and girls. Sustainable development can only be achieved if all people enjoy equal participation in society. That is why we are increasing the share of projects funding to promote gender equality in German development cooperation to at least 93% by 2030. And this is having an impact. If we invest in advancing an equal division of care work, this benefits women in particular. At the same time, it creates leverage for other SDGs, more space for education, work and participation, and stronger social cohesion. Sustainable development can only be achieved if we cooperate at the global level. That is why Germany is continuing to work with determination to implement the 2030 Agenda and will actively advance an ambitious post-2030 framework. In all that, the essential goals of the 2030 Agenda, the principles of leaving no one behind, the whole-of-society approach, and the universality of the goals are important to us. There is a need for honest partnerships that are rooted in respect and reciprocity. Partnerships that are guided by our shared interest: achieving a life in dignity for all. But there is something else. Where opinions differ, it is important to achieve compromises to ensure that all sides can benefit. And to that end, Germany wants to launch a continuous dialogue with representatives from countries in the Global North and the Global South in the context of the NLHLPF and beyond. Sustainable development is a shared responsibility. And with that, I would like to hand over to Marie-Luise Abschagen for the stakeholder statement.

Thank you very much. Excellencies, distinguished guests, I'm speaking to you as a representative of a group of German stakeholders which includes civil society organizations, youth representatives, trade unions, business and industry, science, as well as local communities and municipalities. We are united By our commitments to sustainable development, global justice, and the willingness to build consensus, we want to signal: It is possible to have different perspectives and still constructively cooperate. We would like to thank the German government for giving us the opportunity to be part of the presentation of its third VNR. The government has taken important steps towards improving its policy coherence for sustainable development. Yet it fails to fully integrate the SDGs into its policies. In the spillover score of the STSN, Germany ranks among the 25 worst out of 166 countries. The government must ensure that negative effects of their policies are measured, managed, and stopped, while positive effects contribute to the efforts of other countries in achieving the SDGs. To this end, we urge the government to advocate for globally harmonized standards and governance frameworks for sustainable and circular economy, human and labor rights, decent work, environmental protection, and economic resilience across supply chains. Furthermore, global challenges have impacts at local level. A favorable political framework, sufficient resources, and a genuine multilevel governance are essential for successful transformation. A truly just transition with sustainable and inclusive growth must result in well-being and and tangible improvements in the quality of life and working conditions of people around the world, especially for the most vulnerable and marginalized groups. Today, these promises have only partially been realized, increasingly jeopardizing public support for the necessary transformational changes. We are only at the beginning of multipolar crises. The triple planetary crisis—climate breakdown, Biodiversity loss and pollution hits hardest where responsibility for it is lowest. People of the global majority are facing and feeling the impacts of climate change, debt, violent conflicts, shrinking spaces, and wealth inequality the strongest. Decision-making yet remains with those who are unwilling or unable to take much-needed steps. In the midst of these overlapping pressures, young people try to flourish in a world shaped by ecological collapse, and political inertia. Despite all this, they expected to stay hopeful and innovative. Germany bears responsibility for its own citizens and for people worldwide. A country that leaves no one behind must listen to those it often ignores—its youth and other marginalized groups. It must be in all of our common interest to support the SDGs, reduce inequalities, and ensure a sustainable, dignified, and peaceful life for all people and generations. Thank you.

I thank the Parliamentary State Secretary to the Federal Minister for Economic Cooperation and Development of Germany and the Parliamentary State Secretary to the Federal Ministry for the Environment, Climate Action, Nature Conservation, and Nuclear Safety of Germany and their team for these presentations. Your Excellency, you have the floor.

Mr. Chair, Your Excellencies, distinguished delegates, It is an honor to welcome you all to this important gathering dedicated to the Sustainable Development Goals. Let me start my presentation with a short video dedicated to the way of implementation of SDGs. Abai taught justice, hard work, and the importance of education. These values remain the foundation of sustainable development today. Kazakhstan is showing steady progress. Key strategic documents have been adopted, from the Carbon Neutrality Strategy until 2060 to the new Water Code. In 2025, the UN has supported the President's initiative to establish a regional SDG Center for Central Asia and Afghanistan. Abai's words remain deeply relevant today: "Be merciful, show compassion, avoid evil." These timeless messages are our moral compass. We hear every voice, from the hopes of the youth to the wisdom of the older generation. The Law on Public Oversight, the participatory budgeting mechanism, and digital platforms for citizen engagement—all are tools of open dialogue and a reflection of the core our SDG principle: Leave No One Behind. In 2023, the Parliamentary Commission on the SDGs was established, completing the institutional architecture for sustainable development in the country. The well-being of our citizens is our top priority. The poverty rate has been reduced to 4.8%. A digital family map has been introduced to provide targeted support and assistance. The health of every individual is at the heart of our efforts. Kazakhstan ranks among the top 10 countries with the fastest decline in maternal mortality. We have the lowest neonatal mortality rate in Central Asia—3.4 per 1,000 live births. Concrete steps have been taken to protect women's rights. Penalties for domestic violence have been strengthened. There are 46 crisis centers and 112 family support centers operating across the country. Women's economic and political participation continues to grow. We believe in the potential of our people. In 2024, GDP growth reached 4.8%. Unemployment fell to 4.7%. A Safe Work concept has been adopted. Responsible consumption is our duty to nature. The Environmental Code and the Public Procurement Law now incorporate ESG principles. Over 80% of major companies have already adopted these standards. Abai's wisdom is not a thing of the past. It is a living legacy that inspires us, the new generation. We are building a just, sustainable, and inclusive Kazakhstan. A future where no one is left behind. Thank you very much. Today's presentation of the Third Voluntary National Review of Republic of Kazakhstan is more than just a report. It reflects our commitment to build a more just, inclusive, and Resilient Future. We'll review the progress made, the challenges we faced, and the steps we must take to accelerate the achievement of SDGs in Kazakhstan. Since the previous review, Kazakhstan has taken important steps to nationalize and institutionalize the SDGs. Kazakhstan continues the localization of SDGs. Our national list consists of of 200 indicators, 69 are recognized as relevant and 131 are used for monitoring. In 2024, the methodology of on-SDGs localization was adopted. Since 2023, the Parliamentary Commission on the SDGs has been functioning. The listening state concept plays a special role in our model as practical mechanism for implementing the Leave No One Behind principle. Preparation of the current review has been truly inclusive. The government authorities, parliament, business, civil society, youth organizations, academia, and the UN system partners were involved in the process. We actively used digital tools. Nearly 5,000 people participated in the online survey and consultations. 600 school students shared their vision of the SDGs by participating in national essay contest. Young people are particularly concerned about justice and strong institutions, health, quality education, climate change, and environmental issues. Kazakhstan priorities in the area of SDGs align with the UN Global Goals. Based on the results of the work carried out to involve the population, priority goals for Kazakhstan have been identified. In this regard, detailed information of the 3 objectives is also provided. Kazakhstan implements a wide range of social initiatives. Liability of violence against the children and women has been toughened. A digital family card has been introduced, an innovative tool enabling the delivery of proactive social support measures to the population. The National Fund for Children program was launched. 50% of investment income from the fund is allocated to each child for housing or education. SOS, the UNIFEED, Voluntary educational savings system Kelişek has been launched, ensuring equal access to the educational and opportunities for lifelong learning. Our policy focuses on creating a productive economy and high-quality jobs. A positive dynamics in GDP per capita has been observed. The Aula Manate program has opened access to microloans at 2.5% for residents of villages and small towns. We have implemented a digital map of enterprises which enables tracking of employment dynamics and working conditions. Environmental sustainability is one of the priorities. The principles of sustainability have been incorporated into the public procurement law. We supported the WTO agreement of fish subsidies. Aimed at ending illegal fishing. The Law of Aquaculture has been adopted. The volume of sturgeon stocking increased from 338,000 to 375,000 fish. Kazakhstan is actively developing institutions of rule of law and anti-corruption. All citizens now have direct access to the Constitutional Court, which has been established as a key mechanism for protecting rights and freedoms. To date, the Court has issued over 500 rulings and 71 final decisions. In 20% of reviewed cases, legal provisions were found to be unconstitutional. Free plans adopted at the level of head of state and the government, reflects systemic efforts to enhance human rights and the rule of law. A total of 94 actions have been planned, more than 75% of which have already been implemented. This includes adoption in 2024 a law aimed at protecting victims of domestic violence. As a result, the number of crimes against women decreased by 2.5 times, including the both homicides and crimes affecting women's health. In 2023, Kazakhstan ratified two optional protocols, one to the Convention on the Rights of the Child and another to Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Anti-corruption compliance service have been established, a law countering human, human trafficking has been adopted. An extraterritorial jurisdiction system has been introduced, enabling the allocation of the cases among courts regardless of the place of filing. Kazakhstan continues to be a reliable and active partner in the international arena. Over the past 3 years, Kazakhstan has provided humanitarian assistance totaling $11 million to 9 countries, and it in return received support amounting to around $28 million. This is reciprocity and solidarity in action. On March 4th of this year, the UN General Assembly adopted the resolution of establishing the UN Regional Centre of the SDGs for Central Asia and Afghanistan in Almaty. We are on the threshold of a new stage in the implementation of the 2030 Agenda. Kazakhstan has identified its priority areas: first of all, enhancing public awareness and understanding of the SDGs; accelerating the integration of sustainability principles into budget planning; speeding up the localization of SDGs; SOS: Improving Monitoring and Evaluation Mechanism. Despite global challenges, Kazakhstan remains committed to achieving the SDGs. We are convinced that only through joint efforts we can ensure progress for all, leaving no one behind principle. Thank you for your attention.

Thank you, Mr. President. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen. I am honored to present the Republic of Seychelles' Second VNR on the implementation of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. This VNR reflects the voice, vision and values of our people. A people resilient in the face of adversity, determined in the pursuit of progress, and united by a deep respect for our planet. In the heart of the Indian Ocean lies the Republic of Seychelles, a small island developing state with a population of slightly above 122,000. 2,000 people. Seychelles boasts a bold ambition to build a sustainable, inclusive, and resilient future for all its people. Since our 2020 Voluntary National Review, Seychelles has made meaningful strides in aligning our national development with the 2030 Agenda. We remain committed to a development model that uplifts our people protects our environment, and strengthens our resilience. Let us continue building a future that is fair, inclusive, and full of promise for all Seychellois. This is Seychelles' journey towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals. Since our first VNR in 2020, the global landscape has shifted dramatically. For Small Island Developing States, or Large Ocean States like ours, the last 5 years have tested our endurance. Yet we stand here today not with a story of despair, but one with— of innovation, resolve, and hope. Our 2025 VNR tells a story of continued national commitment backed by measurable progress. Number 1, aligning national vision with global goals. We have fully integrated the SDGs into our second National Development Strategy and long-term vision, Vision 2033. The NDS identifies 6 priority areas: good governance, law and order, human capital development, human rights, inclusive growth, and environmental stewardship. These are not abstract ideals. They are our daily compass. Governance and transparency. Seychelles is proud to be ranked the top African country in the 2024 Mo Ibrahim Governance Index and 18th globally in Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index. This reflects our strong commitment to accountable institutions and the rule of law. Health and education. Our universal health coverage index stands at 0.82, reflecting significant improvements in our maternal and infant care. Education reform is ongoing, with the integration of e-skills and digital learning from early childhood to tertiary level, including the development of inclusive education systems and stronger STEM curricula. Economic resilience and the blue economy. Despite global shocks, our economy is recovering, driven by tourism, fisheries, and the emergence of the blue economy. We have enhanced aquaculture initiatives and developed the Sustainable Seychelles label for tourism. These initiatives support value addition, job creation, and marine conservation. Environmental landscape. Seychelles continues to lead globally in ocean governance and conservation. We have protected over 30% of our Exclusive Economic Zone and nearly 50% of our land. Our Long-Term Low Emission Development Strategy targets net zero emissions by 2050 with 25% renewable energy by 2030. Our landmark Blue Bond disaster risk financing strategy and access to the IMF's Resilience and Sustainability Facility reinforce our climate commitment. Social inclusion. The digitization of social protection services has increased support to our most vulnerable. We have expanded programs for persons with disabilities, strengthened labor protections for migrant workers, and launched inclusive education reforms. The Fast Track Card introduced in 2022 ensures better access to services for people with disabilities. SDG financing and data. We are aligning public budgets with SDG targets through SDG budget tagging and our INFF. The National Bureau of Statistics plays a key role in strengthening data system and ensuring evidence-based decision-making. The path has not been easy. We continue to face significant structural and external constraints. Our dependence on tourism and imports exposes us to global shocks. More than 90% of goods consumed in Seychelles are imported. While we have regained economic momentum, diversifying the economy and ensuring food and energy security remain urgent priorities. Despite achieving high income status in 2015, Seychelles faces restricted access to concessional finance. We continue to advocate globally that income classifications should not obscure structural vulnerabilities. Climate finance in particular must be accessible, predictable and fair for SIDS. We contribute less than 0.003% to global greenhouse gas emissions, yet we bear a disproportionate burden. Rising sea levels, extreme weather conditions and biodiversity loss threaten our infrastructure, livelihoods, and ecosystems. The future of our islands depends on decisive global climate action. With a population of just over 122,000, we face an aging population and shrinking labor force. The working age population is projected to decline from 71% to 64% by 2064, while those aged 65 and over will rise from 9% to 24% in the same period. Investing in skills development and youth empowerment is now more critical than ever. Capital expenditure execution lags due to procurement delays and limited technical capacity. In 2022, execution was 61% below budget. We are addressing this through result-based management, stronger project appraisals, and establishment of a public service College. Our response is clear and bold. We will continue to diversify our economy through transformative economic agenda focused on value-added tourism, sustainable agriculture, and blue economy industries. We will modernize our public sector and improve service delivery through digital transformation, strategic human resource planning, and robust governance framework. We will prioritize— inclusive and resilient development, placing health, education and social protection at the heart of our strategy. We will scale up climate action, mitigating emissions, protecting ecosystems and building adaptive capacity for our most vulnerable communities. We will forge stronger regional and global partnership. Our collaboration with the UN systems, including through the UN SDCF, 2024-2028 is vital. We will continue to work with fellow SIDS to champion equity, resilience, and sustainable financing mechanisms. And most importantly, we will ensure that no one is left behind—be it youth, older persons, migrants, people with disabilities. Every Seychellois must share in our nation's journey forward. Strategy. The SDGs offer Seychelles a roadmap, one that aligns local priorities with global aspirations. Investing in sustainability, good governance, and opportunity for all is not just good for Seychelles, it's essential for our shared planet. Our future lies in innovation, resilience, and strong partnerships. As a small island state, we may face big challenges, but we also have powerful lessons to offer to the world. Let us continue moving forward together with unity and determination. From our coasts to our classrooms, from our leaders to our youth, Seychelles stands united in purpose. Guided by the Sustainable Development Goals, we are building a nation that is resilient, inclusive, and bold. Through the 2025 Voluntary National Review, Seychelles presents a story of progress, resilience, and shared responsibility. We are a small island nation, but with big dreams. As we approach the midpoint to 2030, we must renew our resolve. The SDGs are not merely targets, they are the foundation for dignity, prosperity and peace for all. The future we build today must be one of inclusion, innovation and sustainability. Seychelles reaffirms its unwavering commitment to the full implementation of the 2030 Agenda. We may be small in size, but we are large in ambition. We believe that even the smallest voice, when grounded in principle and purpose, can move mountains. Let us work together across borders, across sectors, and across generations to ensure that the world we pass on is worthy of the hopes we hold today. Thank you.

Dear Chair, it's vital that countries like Germany continue presenting at the GLPF on their SDG implementation. We need leadership countries to uphold human rights, including gender equality, just and sustainable development, and strong multilateralism. Germany has long supported the SDGs in the international fora, yet its domestic implementation is lagging, as the Vienna illustrates. Excellencies, let me name two areas where Germany's commitment must get back on track. The German Supply Chain Act is a major achievement for human rights, climate and labor, and gender rights. It combats child labor, protects workers from exploitation, and defends the environment from destruction. The law demonstrates that economic profit can be regulated, and it's thus incomprehensible that the government and the EU seek to weaken and repeal it. Secondly, while the government pledged to implement the outcomes of the fourth FFD conference, it recently cut development cooperation and humanitarian budgets and is shifting away from feminist foreign policy toward misguided security-led narrative. We therefore ask: Does the government truly intend to dilute The Supply Chain Act, and so how does it plan to uphold human rights, labor standards, environmental and climate commitments in supply chain beyond voluntary measures? How does the government intend to move forward on global debt? Will it support UN initiatives such as Framework Convention on Sovereign Debt and Global Tax Convention to harmonize minimum tax rates and boost domestic revenue? Thank you very much.

I thank you.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. At the outset, I would like to commend Germany, Kazakhstan, and Seychelles for their voluntary national reviews. Thank you very much, Mr. President. I thank the Permanent Representative of Vietnam. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Women's Major Group, to be followed by Namibia. Women's Major Group, you have the floor now.

Mr. Chair, civil society recognized Kazakhstan government institutional efforts on the SDGs adapted strategy, coordination platform, and digital monitoring tools. Many citizens have extremely low income. One-third face debt burden. Another half of household budget go to food. The absence of anti-discrimination legislation fuels violence and hate crimes, including against LGBTQ persons. Civic space continues to shrink, and pressure on human rights defenders persists, undermining SDG 16. Environmental risks around the Aral-Caspian Sea, Lake Balkhash, the Semipalatinsk test site, industrial cities are intensified by cumulative climate impact and anthropogenic pressure, weak local programs, and limited community engagement. To achieve the SDGs, Kazakhstan must reform government systems guided by nature-based processes, free from vested economic interests, and based on inclusive public participation, Circular Economic and Climate Resilience Strategy. I thank the distinguished representative of women's major group. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Namibia to be followed by Tunisia. Namibia, you have the floor now.

These harsh realities are therefore negatively impacting our tourism operations, reducing fishery yields, amongst others. Therefore, in order to address them, we require a comprehensive, coordinated, and sustained response at both national and international levels. Therefore, for SIDS like Seychelles, we urgently need development partners to amplify advocacy efforts and build global solidarity for causes such as climate action. At the same time, we now have the opportunity to develop our oil and gas resources, which could generate significant revenue for the country and lift us out of economic difficulties. On one hand, we have our forest, and on the other, we have an opportunity to develop through oil and gas. But how do we combine these? This is where the Green Development Strategy, or GDS, comes into play. The GDS predicts that if we do not if we do not develop a tailor-made strategy to sustainably reinvest the funds we earn from the extractive sector into a sustainable future for Suriname, we would lose our carbon-negative status and our forest cover would be less than 90%. The GDS is a strategy for Suriname focused on developments for now until the year 2050. Its goal is to develop our country in a sustainable and balanced way while achieving several clear and measurable objectives. According to the GDS, Suriname should pursue a high-ambition strategy centered on nature conservation, industrialization supported by a service-driven economy, and fueled by advancements in education and technology. Eventually transitioning to more sustainable sectors such as manufacturing, financial services, ICT, ecotourism, and renewable energy. The GDS foresees that by reducing reliance on harmful small-scale mining practices and using income generated from the oil and gas sector wisely, Suriname can reallocate money towards projects that benefit the economy, society, society and environment in the long run. The Green Development Strategy is more than a plan. It's a vision to build a future where prosperity, nature, and social justice go hand in hand. Over the next 25 years, Suriname will require a total investment of $72.5 billion for the Sustainable Development Vision 2050 projected by the GDB. S, factoring in GDP growth, population trends, and sectoral needs. To finance these sustainable development investment costs for Suriname, a strategic distribution among public funding, international climate and biodiversity finance, and private sector investment is essential. Furthermore, a special fund is to be created from our future oil and gas revenues. The identified financing These financing mechanisms are expected to provide the necessary capital to meet the GDS objectives. This is not just about this government's term or the next. No, we are looking ahead at least 5 government terms and beyond. It is essential for every government to commit to this, regardless of who is in power. To ensure this vision becomes a reality, we will enshrine it in a law, a law that guarantees oil and gas revenues will not be wasted but invested in our people and our future, not only for this generation but for generations to come. This law will provide clear guidelines and a strong framework that the government and future administrations must follow to steer the country in the right direction. This is our shared future. With your support, we will make Suriname a country we can all be proud for ourselves, for our children, and for the world. A better future begins now. Turning now to our PowerPoint presentation. Data is another pillar of our work. Our General Bureau of Statistics and the Planning Office are expanding efforts to improve data—SDG data collection and monitoring with digital tools and more frequent reporting. We are also seeing growing alignment from the private sector and NGOs with the SDG agenda, evidence that this is becoming a whole-of-society effort. Going through the SDGs, we have grouped them together, focusing now on macroeconomic and social welfare focus. Our progress overview starts with: we have recovered from recent economic shocks. Suriname prioritized inflation control, fiscal discipline, and debt restructuring while expanding social assistance programs for the most vulnerable. We have improved access to healthcare, pensions, and labor protection and passed a national minimum wage law that is updated annually. As a result, poverty has dropped from 22% in 2016 from 16% to 18% in 2022, an encouraging trend supported by expanded social support and government-subsidized healthcare. Turning to human capacity and safety, we have reformed our education system by updating curricula, training teachers, and improving infrastructure to better prepare youth for future jobs. To support sustainable livelihoods, we have invested in climate-smart agriculture, vocational training, and SME support, while our Just Transition program is creating new pathways to green jobs. On gender equality, legislative reforms, and tackling discrimination and violence while empowering women to lead. A draft law on collective rights for indigenous and tribal peoples is on the way, a critical step towards inclusive development. To strengthen justice, Suriname has established an anti-corruption commission. Let us now turn to the next important area on Suriname's SDG path: living conditions, infrastructure, and environmental sustainability. Particularly in underserved and remote communities. Suriname is improving infrastructure services and sustainability with a focus on remote areas. Investment in clean water, solar, and hybrid energy, especially in the hinterland. Roads and transport systems are being upgraded. A new spatial planning vision promotes balanced growth and climate resilience. Waste management efforts now include medical and e-waste. Continued strengthening of partnerships at bilateral, regional, and multilateral levels is at the center of Suriname's foreign policy. Moving to biodiversity and environment. Suriname remains one of the few CO2-negative countries in the world. We are proud of this, but it comes with responsibility. We have increased investment in biodiversity, climate policy coordination, and mercury-free mining. The establishment of the National Environment Authority allows for better oversight of climate plans and stakeholder capacity. Turning to Suriname's critical areas of concern, social protection still falls short, particularly for the elderly, persons with disability, and people in remote areas. Gender-based violence remains a serious issue. Climate change is affecting agriculture. Informal sector undermines job security and economic growth. Crime trafficking and money laundering pose rising threats. Our waste policy is just in its infancy. Other critical areas of concern: we need more renewable energy investments, stronger governance and audit institutions, a rights-based approach in policymaking for ITPs, women, LGBTQ+, and persons with disability; promotion of green jobs and support for MSMEs; combating food insecurity with agro-, forestry, and community-based food systems; and Suriname's classification as a high-middle-income country limits access to concessional Financing. What is the way forward? Policy continuity. SDG must remain a guiding principle. Stronger institutions. We need support to further strengthen functional governance systems, train civil servants, and empower the SDG platform and the SDG committee as mechanisms for dialogue and coordination. Thank you, Mr. President. Going to the question of Morocco, regarding oil and gas in relation to our carbon credits. We are proud to be globally recognized for our exceptional forest coverage of 93% over our territory. What will we do? We will embark on the responsible development of oil and gas sector as a means to catalyze economic growth, generate employment, and improve the well-being of our people. We recognize that from the outside, this dual trajectory may appear difficult to reconcile. However, we strongly believe that sustainable development and environmental integrity can and must coexist. How will we do that? We have an independent oversight by the National Environmental Authority, the NMA. Our independent— our NMA is legally mandated to oversee environmental and social impact assessments for all major development projects. This includes all oil and gas operations. The NMA ensures that all offshore activities comply with environmental legislation, follow international best practices, and implement mitigation and monitoring frameworks throughout the project lifecycle. Cycle. Enforceable environmental standard of 10 ppm oil in water discharge limit. Suriname enforces a strict environmental discharge standard of 10 parts per million oil in the water for all offshore oil operations. This is a key safeguard for protecting marine biodiversity and preventing pollution. All companies operating offshore in Suriname, whether national or international, are contractually bound to comply with this standard. This requirement is embedded in their operation agreements and both— and monitored by both the NMA and the state oil company as the National Petroleum Company. Compliance with the 10 ppm limit is non-negotiable. Regardless of cost of implications, and it is monitored daily as part of each operator's environmental performance obligation. Moving to the question of Bhutan regarding economic diversification beyond extractive industries, we recognize that true sustainable development means moving beyond dependence on extractive industries, and ensuring that the benefits of growth reach every community, especially those often left behind. What will we do? A crucial step will be the focus on sectors that generate sustainable jobs, such as agriculture, renewable energy, ecotourism, and sustainable forestry. To protect communities from shocks and setbacks, a strong social protection system must be in place so that everyone has the resilience and security to take part in the country's transformation. To accelerate this progress, Suriname will have to fast-track legislation to recognize indigenous land rights, scale up successful models such as the Innovation Hub for Agriculture, extending its benefits to more crops because now we're only doing pineapple, expand green industries in rural areas, strengthen data systems to monitor progress, deepen community-driven planning, and reinforce social safety nets. On the question of El Salvador regarding gender and equality, We recognize that Article 8 of the Constitution and the Equal Treatment in Labor Law provide important guarantees of equality and non-discrimination, including explicit protection against discrimination on the grounds of sexual inclination, orientation, and gender identity in employment. However, the government acknowledges that despite these legal protections, There remain significant practical gaps in protecting, for example, LGBTI persons in other areas of daily life, particularly healthcare, housing, education, and access to essential services. Stigma and discrimination still prevent many individuals from accessing timely medical care, secure housing, or accurate sexual health education. Why— which undermines efforts to meet the targets. To address these gaps, the government, through the Bureau for Gender Affairs, and in close cooperation with civil society and development partners, will strengthen enforcement mechanisms to ensure compliance with existing anti-discrimination laws, advance inclusive healthcare policies, improve the educational system capacity to deliver comprehensive and consistent sexual education, address housing discrimination through new guidelines, ensure adequate budget allocation for sexual and reproductive health rights.
